title: After Joshua: An Unfinished Conquest
summary: After Joshua's death, Judah leads the tribes in fighting for their territories and wins victories at Bezek, Jerusalem, Hebron, and Debir, where Othniel wins Caleb's daughter Acsah. But the chapter turns into a list of failures, as tribe after tribe, from Benjamin to Dan, does not drive out the Canaanites, and many are left living among Israel or put to forced labor.
story: Joshua ended with the land allotted and the people pledging at Shechem to serve the LORD. Judges opens with a new situation: Joshua is dead, and there is no single leader. Each tribe must take its own territory, and the book asks what kind of people Israel will be when the generation that saw God's great acts is gone. This chapter is the military side of the answer. It starts with confidence (the LORD tells Judah to go first) and slides steadily toward compromise, setting up the spiritual diagnosis of chapter 2. The Canaanites who remain here become the snare that Joshua warned about in Joshua 23:13.
historical:
The setting is the early Iron Age in Canaan, around the twelfth century BC on the more common reckoning (earlier on the view that the exodus took place in the fifteenth century BC). Several of the places named are well known from archaeology and other ancient texts. Megiddo, Taanach, Beth-shean, and Gezer were fortified Canaanite cities guarding the major valleys and trade routes, and Beth-shean was an Egyptian garrison center in the Late Bronze Age and into the early Iron Age. These cities sat on the plains where chariots could operate, which explains why Israel, a people of the hill country, struggled to take them. Gezer did not become Israelite until a pharaoh captured it and gave it to Solomon as a dowry (1 Kings 9:16).

The chapter also overlaps with Joshua: the capture of Hebron and Debir and the story of Acsah appear in Joshua 15:13-19, and the notice that the Jebusites remained in Jerusalem appears in Joshua 15:63. Jerusalem is burned by Judah here (verse 8), yet Jebusites still live there (verse 21), and the city was not firmly held by Israel until David took it (2 Samuel 5:6-9). Most scholars think Judah raided or burned the city but did not hold it. Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron (verse 18) later became Philistine strongholds; the ancient Greek translation (the Septuagint) reads this verse as saying Judah did not take them.
cultural:
Cutting off a captive king's thumbs and big toes (verses 6 and 7) left him unable to hold a weapon or run into battle, and it humiliated him publicly. Adoni-bezek (his name means lord of Bezek) had done the same to seventy lesser kings, who were likely local rulers of small city-states. His own words interpret his fate as just repayment, and the narrator lets his confession stand.

Acsah's request shows how land and water worked in the Negev, the dry south. Land without springs was nearly worthless for farming. A daughter's marriage often came with a gift from her father, and Acsah's boldness secures her family's survival. The Kenites (verse 16) were a clan related to Moses' father-in-law who settled among Judah; the City of Palms was Jericho (Deuteronomy 34:3). Forced labor (verses 28 to 35) meant that conquered peoples were put to work on building and farming for the stronger group, a common practice in the ancient world. The Law had commanded Israel to drive out the Canaanites and not make agreements with them (Deuteronomy 7:1-5), so turning them into laborers was a compromise that looked like strength.
literary: The chapter is a report of the conquest arranged by tribe, moving roughly from south to north: Judah and Simeon first, then Benjamin, the house of Joseph, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali, and finally Dan. As it moves, the tone darkens. Judah's section is mostly success; the northern tribes' sections are mostly failure. The key phrase shifts from the LORD being with Judah to the refrain that a tribe did not drive out the inhabitants. There is also a shift in who lives among whom: first the Canaanites live among Israel (verse 29), then Israel lives among the Canaanites (verse 32), and finally Dan is pushed back by the Amorites (verse 34). Acsah's small story stands out as a picture of what Israel could have been: a people who ask boldly and receive the blessing of land and water.

outline.t: Israel asks the LORD, and Judah goes up with Simeon
Victory at Bezek and the fate of Adoni-bezek
Jerusalem, the hill country, and Hebron
Othniel takes Debir, and Acsah asks for springs
The Kenites, Hormah, the coast, and the limits of Judah's success
The house of Joseph takes Bethel
Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, and Naphtali fail to drive out the Canaanites
Dan is pushed back by the Amorites

doctrines.note: The land was God's covenant gift, and taking it fully was Israel's covenant task. The chapter shows the gap between what God gave and what Israel was willing to receive.
Adoni-bezek's confession that God has repaid him as he had done to others expresses a principle Scripture repeats: God's justice often answers wrongdoing in kind.
The failures accumulate quietly. There is no dramatic rebellion here, only a series of accommodations. Chapter 2 will reveal that this drift was disobedience.

words.note: Yarash, to take possession, or to drive out and dispossess. It is the key verb of the chapter, and it is almost always negated in the second half: tribe after tribe did not drive out the inhabitants. The same word describes Israel inheriting the land, so failing to drive out is also failing to possess.

Mas, forced labor or a labor gang. When Israel grew strong, it made the Canaanites into laborers rather than removing them. The word later describes the labor gangs Solomon conscripted, including Israelites (1 Kings 5:13). Here it marks a compromise that served Israel's comfort rather than God's command.
Berakhah, blessing. Acsah's request, give me a blessing, uses the word for a gift that brings life and prosperity. In a chapter of failures, she is the one who asks for more and receives it.

Charam, to devote to destruction, to set something apart for God by giving it up entirely. The town Zephath becomes Hormah, a name built from the same root, recalling the earlier vow of Numbers 21:1-3.

christ: Judah, the tribe God chooses to go first (verse 2), is the tribe from which David and his royal line will come, and from which the New Testament traces Jesus (Matthew 1:2-3, Hebrews 7:14). The book's first word about leadership already leans toward that tribe. More broadly, the chapter shows a people who received a promised inheritance and did not fully enter it, a theme the letter to the Hebrews takes up when it speaks of a rest God's people must still enter (Hebrews 4:1-11). The connection is thematic: Israel's half-possessed land points toward the full inheritance that the New Testament says is secured in Christ (1 Peter 1:3-4).

hard.q: How can the LORD be with Judah and yet Judah cannot drive out people with iron chariots?
hard.a: Verse 19 is uncomfortable, since it seems to say that God's presence was not enough. Some readers take it as a straightforward military observation: hill-country infantry could not fight chariots on open plains. Others note that Joshua had promised Israel would drive out the Canaanites even though they had iron chariots (Joshua 17:18), and read verse 19 as quietly exposing a failure of trust rather than a limit on God. The chapter's movement toward failure and the rebuke in 2:1-3 support the second reading, but the first is also part of the picture: the narrator reports what Israel could not do, and chapter 2 explains why.

questions: Acsah asked for more than she had been given, and received it. What would it look like to ask God boldly for what you need?
The tribes chose forced labor over obedience because it seemed practical. Where are you tempted to call a compromise wisdom?
The chapter begins with Israel asking the LORD what to do. Why do you think the asking disappears as the chapter goes on?
